topics.title: Dense graph classes
topics.description: Transductions, monadic dependence, and the definitions and relationships of graph widths.

questions.prompt: Fix finitely many unary predicates and FO formulas $\delta(x),\varphi(x,y)$, with $\varphi$ symmetric and irreflexive. Arbitrarily interpret the predicates on $G$, select vertices by $\delta$, and define adjacency by $\varphi$. What is this set-valued operation, with no copying?

answers.text: A non-copying first-order transduction.
answers.explanation: The formulas and predicate vocabulary are fixed; the unary expansions vary. Each expansion yields an interpreted graph, so one input can have several outputs.

answers.text: A graph homomorphism.
answers.explanation: A homomorphism maps vertices while preserving edges; it does not redefine adjacency by arbitrary FO formulas.

answers.text: A graph minor operation.
answers.explanation: Minor operations delete or contract edges and vertices; an FO transduction can also create edges.

answers.text: A graph isomorphism.
answers.explanation: An isomorphism preserves the whole adjacency relation bijectively. Here both the domain and adjacency may change.

answers.text: A deterministic interpretation of the uncoloured graph alone.
answers.explanation: The arbitrary unary expansions are extra choices, so the output is not determined by the uncoloured input alone.

answers.text: A vertex-colouring operation with adjacency unchanged.
answers.explanation: Colouring is only the preparatory step; the formulas can also change edges and select a domain.

answers.text: An arbitrary MSO transduction requiring vertex-set quantifiers in its defining formulas.
answers.explanation: The defining formulas here are first-order. Unary parameters do not make their quantifiers second-order.

answers.text: A quotient interpretation whose output vertices must be equivalence classes.
answers.explanation: The selected vertices are individual input vertices; this convention includes no quotient operation.

answers.text: A two-dimensional interpretation whose output vertices must be ordered pairs.
answers.explanation: Here the domain formula has one free variable. Output vertices are not pairs of input vertices.

answers.text: A copying transduction with an unbounded input-dependent number of copies.
answers.explanation: No copies occur here; even in the copying convention the copy number is a fixed constant.

questions.prompt: How does a non-copying FO transduction with domain formula $\delta$ and symmetric, irreflexive edge formula $\varphi$ construct an output $H$ from a unary expansion $G^+$?

answers.text: $V(H)=\{v:G^+\models\delta(v)\}$; for $u,v\in V(H)$, $uv\in E(H)\iff G^+\models\varphi(u,v)$.
answers.explanation: Evaluate both fixed formulas in the expanded input. The domain formula selects output vertices; the edge formula determines adjacency between them.

answers.text: $V(H)=V(G)$; retain exactly the original edges, regardless of $\delta$ and $\varphi$.
answers.explanation: This ignores both defining formulas and cannot describe a general transduction.

answers.text: $V(H)=\{v:G^+\models\varphi(v,v)\}$; adjacency is determined by $\delta(u)\land\delta(v)$.
answers.explanation: The edge formula is irreflexive, so its diagonal is empty. The roles of the domain and edge formulas are reversed.

answers.text: $V(H)=E(G)$; join two output vertices when the corresponding input edges meet.
answers.explanation: That describes the line-graph construction, not this one-dimensional vertex-domain definition.

answers.text: $V(H)=\{v:G^+\models\delta(v)\}$; keep only input edges that also satisfy $\varphi$.
answers.explanation: An FO edge formula may create an edge that was absent from the input. Intersecting with the old edge set is an extra restriction.

answers.text: $V(H)=\{v:G^+\models\delta(v)\}$; test $\varphi$ only in $G^+[V(H)]$.
answers.explanation: Quantified variables of the edge formula range over the input structure. Deleting unselected witnesses first can change its truth.

answers.text: $V(H)=\{v:G^+\models\delta(v)\}$; evaluate $\varphi$ after forgetting all added predicates.
answers.explanation: The edge formula is allowed to use those unary predicates.

answers.text: Use the stated domain, but require $\varphi(u,v)$ in every unary expansion of $G$.
answers.explanation: Each individual expansion can produce its own output. Taking the intersection over all expansions changes the operation.

answers.text: Use the stated domain, but choose a separate unary expansion for each pair $u,v$.
answers.explanation: One expansion must determine the entire output graph, not a different expansion for each potential edge.

answers.text: Use the stated domain, but evaluate $\varphi$ in the output graph $H$ itself.
answers.explanation: The formulas are evaluated in the input expansion. Evaluating them recursively in the output is not this definition.

questions.prompt: For graph classes $\mathcal C,\mathcal D$, what does $\mathcal D\subseteq T(\mathcal C)$ require of a single fixed FO transduction $T$?

answers.text: One fixed finite vocabulary and fixed formulas work for every $H\in\mathcal D$; the chosen $G\in\mathcal C$ and its colouring may depend on $H$.
answers.explanation: Uniformity concerns the recipe, not the input graph or colouring. Every target must occur among the outputs of that one recipe.

answers.text: Every $G\in\mathcal C$ must produce every $H\in\mathcal D$.
answers.explanation: Class transducibility only requires some suitable input for each target.

answers.text: One finite $G\in\mathcal C$ must produce all graphs of every order in $\mathcal D$.
answers.explanation: A fixed finite input has bounded output size. The input is allowed to vary with the target.

answers.text: The defining formula may be chosen separately for each target $H$.
answers.explanation: That discards the fixed-recipe requirement.

answers.text: The formulas are fixed, but the number of unary predicates may grow with the target.
answers.explanation: The finite predicate vocabulary is also part of the fixed transduction.

answers.text: The vocabulary is fixed, but quantifier rank may grow through a new formula for each target.
answers.explanation: A fixed transduction uses fixed formulas, hence a fixed quantifier rank.

answers.text: The recipe must generate exactly $\mathcal D$ and no additional outputs.
answers.explanation: The definition asks for containment in the outputs, not equality.

answers.text: Each target uses one recipe for vertices and unrelated input graphs for its individual edges.
answers.explanation: The whole output is interpreted in a single expanded input graph.

answers.text: The unary predicates must be FO-definable in the uncoloured input.
answers.explanation: They are arbitrary unary parameters, not predicates required to be definable without parameters.

answers.text: The formulas and one fixed colouring assignment must work unchanged on all input graphs.
answers.explanation: The formulas are uniform, but colour assignments are chosen separately on each input vertex set.

questions.prompt: In the convention allowing copying, how is a $k$-copy operation used in an FO transduction?

answers.text: Use a fixed $k$, distinguish the copies, and link corresponding copies of each original vertex before the fixed FO interpretation.
answers.explanation: Copying supplies finitely many tagged copies and a correspondence relation. The constant and interpretation belong to the transduction, not to individual inputs.

answers.text: Take $|V(G)|$ copies and choose new defining formulas for each input.
answers.explanation: Both an input-dependent copy number and input-dependent formulas violate the fixed-transduction convention.

answers.text: Replace every vertex by all subsets of the input vertex set.
answers.explanation: A fixed-copy operation gives only a constant-factor increase, not a powerset domain.

answers.text: Contract every connected component before interpreting the graph.
answers.explanation: Copying duplicates vertices; it is not a component quotient.

answers.text: Take a fixed number of untagged copies and erase which vertices correspond.
answers.explanation: The standard copying structure supplies copy tags and the correspondence relation for the formulas to use.

answers.text: Allow arbitrarily many copies as long as the edge formula is fixed.
answers.explanation: The copy number itself must also be fixed.

answers.text: Use a fixed number of copies, but require the output to contain every copied vertex.
answers.explanation: The subsequent interpretation may select a smaller domain.

answers.text: Use a fixed number of copies, but forbid formulas from relating different copies.
answers.explanation: The correspondence relation and copy tags are supplied precisely so cross-copy relationships can be defined.

answers.text: Use a fixed number of copies, identified into one equivalence class per original vertex before any formula is evaluated.
answers.explanation: That collapses the copies before interpretation. Standard copying retains the distinct copies as available elements.

answers.text: Use a fixed number of copies only when all unary parameters are already definable in the original graph.
answers.explanation: Arbitrary finitely many unary parameters are allowed; definability in the original graph is not required.

questions.prompt: A class $\mathcal C$ cannot produce every finite simple graph by any one fixed FO transduction, even with arbitrary finitely many unary vertex predicates. What is this property called?

answers.text: Monadic dependence (monadic NIP).
answers.explanation: The forbidden encoding is a single uniform recipe for all finite graphs. Unary expansions account for the word “monadic”.

answers.text: Bounded clique-width.
answers.explanation: Bounded clique-width implies this property, but its definition uses labelled graph expressions and is stronger.

answers.text: Bounded twin-width.
answers.explanation: Twin-width is defined by contraction sequences. Monadic dependence also includes classes with unbounded twin-width.

answers.text: Bounded shrubdepth.
answers.explanation: Shrubdepth requires uniformly bounded tree-model height and colour count, a stronger condition.

answers.text: Monadic independence.
answers.explanation: Independence is the opposite: some fixed transduction does encode all finite graphs.

answers.text: Monadic stability.
answers.explanation: Stability forbids transducing all half-graphs, not merely all finite graphs; it is stronger.

answers.text: Nowhere denseness.
answers.explanation: Nowhere denseness is a sparse structural property; monadic dependence also permits arbitrarily large cliques.

answers.text: Bounded merge-width.
answers.explanation: Bounded merge-width controls each radius by a constant. Monadic dependence need only yield almost bounded merge-width.

answers.text: Bounded VC-dimension of the adjacency relation alone.
answers.explanation: Monadic dependence controls every fixed FO encoding after unary expansions, not only raw adjacency.

answers.text: Exclusion of one finite graph as an induced subgraph.
answers.explanation: An induced-subgraph exclusion alone does not prevent logical encodings of all graphs.

questions.prompt: Let $\mathcal G$ be all finite simple graphs and $T$ range over fixed FO transductions with unary parameters. Which condition defines monadic dependence of $\mathcal C$?

answers.text: $\forall T\;\exists H\in\mathcal G:\ H\notin T(\mathcal C)$.
answers.explanation: Every fixed recipe misses at least one finite graph. The graph it misses may depend on the recipe.

answers.text: $\exists T\;\forall H\in\mathcal G:\ H\in T(\mathcal C)$.
answers.explanation: This is monadic independence, the negation of dependence.

answers.text: $\forall T\;\forall H\in\mathcal G:\ H\notin T(\mathcal C)$.
answers.explanation: This forbids even trivial outputs; dependence only requires each recipe to miss some graph.

answers.text: $\exists T\;\exists H\in\mathcal G:\ H\notin T(\mathcal C)$.
answers.explanation: One weak transduction missing a graph says nothing about another transduction encoding all graphs.

answers.text: $\exists H\in\mathcal G\;\forall T:\ H\notin T(\mathcal C)$.
answers.explanation: This swaps the quantifiers. For example, large cliques can encode any one fixed finite graph using finitely many colours tailored to that graph.

answers.text: $\forall H\in\mathcal G\;\exists T:\ H\notin T(\mathcal C)$.
answers.explanation: Choosing a deliberately unhelpful transduction separately for each target does not rule out a universal encoding.

answers.text: $\forall T\;\exists G\in\mathcal C\;\exists H\in\mathcal G:\ H\notin T(G)$.
answers.explanation: Failure on one input is insufficient: the target might be produced from another input in the class.

answers.text: $\forall T\;\exists H\in\mathcal G:\ H\notin T(\mathcal C)$, but only for transductions without unary parameters.
answers.explanation: Removing unary parameters weakens the test. Monadic dependence explicitly allows arbitrary finite unary expansions.

answers.text: $\forall T\;\exists H\in\mathcal G:\ H\notin T(\mathcal C)$, but only for quantifier-free edge formulas.
answers.explanation: All first-order formulas must be considered, not just quantifier-free ones.

answers.text: $\forall G\in\mathcal C\;\forall T\;\exists H\in\mathcal G:\ H\notin T(G)$.
answers.explanation: Every fixed finite input has bounded output size. This holds even for the class of all finite graphs.

questions.prompt: Let $\mathcal C$ be monadically dependent and let $\mathcal D\subseteq T(\mathcal C)$ for a fixed FO transduction $T$. What follows?

answers.text: $\mathcal D$ is monadically dependent: a universal encoding from $\mathcal D$ would compose with $T$ to give one from $\mathcal C$.
answers.explanation: FO transductions compose. If a transduction of the output class encoded all graphs, the composition would contradict dependence of the input class.

answers.text: $\mathcal D$ must be monadically independent, because a transduction adds arbitrary colours.
answers.explanation: Arbitrary colours are already allowed in the definition of monadic dependence.

answers.text: $\mathcal D$ must have bounded shrubdepth, regardless of $\mathcal C$.
answers.explanation: The identity transduction on all paths disproves this: paths are monadically dependent but have unbounded shrubdepth.

answers.text: $\mathcal D$ must have bounded clique-width, regardless of $\mathcal C$.
answers.explanation: The identity on planar grids disproves this: they are dependent but have unbounded clique-width.

answers.text: Dependence follows only when $T$ is injective on isomorphism classes.
answers.explanation: The composition argument needs no injectivity.

answers.text: Dependence follows only when $T$ never changes adjacency.
answers.explanation: Composition works for arbitrary allowed edge formulas, including complementation.

answers.text: Dependence follows only when $\mathcal D=T(\mathcal C)$.
answers.explanation: A subclass of a dependent class is dependent; containment is sufficient.

answers.text: Dependence follows only when $\mathcal C$ is closed under arbitrary subgraphs.
answers.explanation: The composition argument requires no subgraph-closure assumption.

answers.text: Dependence follows only when each input has a unique output under $T$.
answers.explanation: Set-valued transductions still compose; unary choices can be encoded together.

answers.text: Dependence follows only when $T$ has quantifier-free formulas.
answers.explanation: Fixed first-order formulas are closed under the substitutions used in composition.

questions.prompt: Merge two parts at each step, from singletons to $\{V(G)\}$. Join distinct parts by a red edge exactly when their original adjacency is neither complete nor empty. Minimise the largest red degree over the entire sequence. Which parameter is this?

answers.text: Twin-width.
answers.explanation: Red edges record non-homogeneous pairs of parts. The width is a maximum degree over all intermediate red graphs, minimised over binary merge sequences.

answers.text: Clique-width.
answers.explanation: Clique-width minimises labels in a graph-building expression, not red degree during contractions.

answers.text: Treewidth.
answers.explanation: Treewidth uses bags in a tree decomposition; it is not defined by this merging process.

answers.text: Shrubdepth.
answers.explanation: Shrubdepth concerns bounded-height, bounded-colour tree-models for a class.

answers.text: Rank-width.
answers.explanation: Rank-width minimises the maximum binary rank of adjacency matrices across decomposition cuts.

answers.text: Neighbourhood diversity.
answers.explanation: Neighbourhood diversity counts twin classes in one partition; it does not optimise an entire contraction sequence.

answers.text: Radius-1 merge-width.
answers.explanation: Merge-width counts parts reached through resolved pairs of original vertices, not red degree between current parts.

answers.text: Component twin-width.
answers.explanation: Component twin-width bounds the size of red connected components, rather than their maximum degree.

answers.text: Linear clique-width.
answers.explanation: Linear clique-width restricts labelled construction expressions to adding one vertex at a time.

answers.text: Radius-infinity merge-width.
answers.explanation: That parameter counts reachable parts in resolved-pair components and is equivalent in boundedness to clique-width.

questions.prompt: Let $R_i$ be the red graph at step $i$ of a valid contraction sequence $\sigma$ from a finite nonempty graph $G$ to one vertex. Which formula defines $\operatorname{tww}(G)$? Here $\Delta$ is maximum degree.

answers.text: $\min_{\sigma}\max_i\Delta(R_i)$.
answers.explanation: Choose the best sequence, but control the worst red degree at every stage and every current vertex.

answers.text: $\max_{\sigma}\max_i\Delta(R_i)$.
answers.explanation: Twin-width optimises over the choice of sequence; it does not use the worst possible sequence.

answers.text: $\min_{\sigma}\min_i\Delta(R_i)$.
answers.explanation: The first and last red graphs are edgeless, so this would always be zero.

answers.text: $\min_{\sigma}\sum_i\Delta(R_i)$.
answers.explanation: The definition bounds the peak, not the sum of red degrees over time.

answers.text: $\min_{\sigma}\max_i|E(R_i)|$.
answers.explanation: Total red-edge count can be large while every red degree stays small.

answers.text: $\min_{\sigma}\max_i|V(R_i)|$.
answers.explanation: The initial graph already has all input vertices; counting them measures input size rather than contraction errors.

answers.text: $\min_{\sigma}\max_i\Delta(B_i)$, where $B_i$ contains only black edges.
answers.explanation: Twin-width bounds red uncertainty. Black adjacency can be arbitrarily dense, as in a clique.

answers.text: $\min_{\sigma}\max_i\operatorname{avgdeg}(R_i)$.
answers.explanation: An average can hide a vertex with large red degree. The bound must hold at every vertex.

answers.text: $\min_{\sigma}\max_i\max\{|C|:C\text{ is a component of }R_i\}$.
answers.explanation: This bounds red component size, a stronger and different width measure.

answers.text: $\min_{\sigma}\max_i\Delta(R_i)$, with $\sigma$ restricted to merging adjacent vertices.
answers.explanation: Standard twin-width allows identification of nonadjacent vertices too; an edgeless graph must still admit a sequence.

questions.prompt: In a trigraph contraction, merge $u,v$ into $w$ and consider another vertex $x$. Write $B,N,R$ for black edge, non-edge, and red edge. What is the status of $wx$?

answers.text: $BB\mapsto B$, $NN\mapsto N$; every other pair of statuses maps to $R$.
answers.explanation: Both parts must agree definitely to yield a definite edge or non-edge. Any disagreement or inherited uncertainty stays red.

answers.text: $BB\mapsto B$, $NN\mapsto N$, $BN\mapsto N$; inherited red edges stay red.
answers.explanation: An edge/non-edge disagreement must become red; choosing non-edge loses the discrepancy.

answers.text: $BB\mapsto B$, $NN\mapsto N$, $BN\mapsto B$; inherited red edges stay red.
answers.explanation: Taking the union of neighbourhoods hides an edge/non-edge disagreement instead of recording it.

answers.text: Every status pair maps to $R$.
answers.explanation: Agreement of two black edges stays black, and agreement of two non-edges stays a non-edge.

answers.text: $BB\mapsto B$, $NN\mapsto N$, $BN\mapsto R$; $RR\mapsto N$.
answers.explanation: Two red incidences do not cancel their inherited uncertainty.

answers.text: $BB\mapsto B$, $NN\mapsto N$, $BN\mapsto R$; $BR\mapsto B$.
answers.explanation: A black edge does not resolve the uncertainty inherited from the red edge.

answers.text: $BB\mapsto B$, $NN\mapsto N$, $BN\mapsto R$; $NR\mapsto N$.
answers.explanation: A definite non-edge does not resolve uncertainty from a red incidence.

answers.text: $BB\mapsto R$, $NN\mapsto N$; every remaining pair maps to $R$.
answers.explanation: Two complete adjacency relations combine into another complete relation, so black plus black is black.

answers.text: $BB\mapsto B$, $NN\mapsto R$; every remaining pair maps to $R$.
answers.explanation: Two empty adjacency relations combine into an empty relation, so non-edge plus non-edge stays a non-edge.

answers.text: Equal statuses are preserved; unequal statuses map to the status of $ux$.
answers.explanation: The merge is symmetric in its two inputs. Different definite statuses must produce red, independent of order.

questions.prompt: Which parameter is the minimum number of labels needed to build $G$ using labelled single vertices, disjoint union, complete joins between two distinct labels, and global relabelling?

answers.text: Clique-width.
answers.explanation: Labels are reusable construction states. The parameter counts how many labels suffice for an expression, not the size of a clique.

answers.text: Clique number.
answers.explanation: Clique number is the size of a largest complete subgraph; it does not count construction labels.

answers.text: Chromatic number.
answers.explanation: Construction labels need not form independent sets and are not a proper colouring.

answers.text: Twin-width.
answers.explanation: Twin-width is measured by red degrees along contractions.

answers.text: Treewidth.
answers.explanation: Treewidth counts bag size minus one in a tree decomposition.

answers.text: Shrubdepth.
answers.explanation: Shrubdepth also constrains depth through a tree-model; unrestricted expression height is allowed here.

answers.text: Neighbourhood diversity.
answers.explanation: Construction labels can be reused and changed; final twin classes need not correspond to one fixed global labelling.

answers.text: Linear clique-width.
answers.explanation: Linear clique-width additionally restricts disjoint union so that only one vertex is added at a time.

answers.text: NLC-width.
answers.explanation: NLC-width uses a different join-and-union operation, with edges added between the two operands according to a label-pair relation.

answers.text: Rank-width.
answers.explanation: Rank-width uses binary adjacency-matrix ranks across cuts, rather than this expression syntax.

questions.prompt: Which operation is permitted by a standard $k$-expression for clique-width?

answers.text: For $i\ne j$, add every missing edge between the current label-$i$ and label-$j$ vertices.
answers.explanation: A join acts uniformly on two distinct label classes. It adds edges and leaves existing edges in place.

answers.text: Delete an arbitrary existing edge while preserving all labels.
answers.explanation: Edge deletion is not a primitive operation of a clique-width expression.

answers.text: Identify any two vertices of the same label.
answers.explanation: Clique-width expressions build graphs without contracting vertices.

answers.text: Add just one chosen edge between two otherwise indistinguishable labelled vertices.
answers.explanation: A join treats entire label classes uniformly, not chosen individual vertices within them.

answers.text: Complement adjacency between two label classes in one primitive step.
answers.explanation: The join adds all missing edges; it does not toggle or remove existing edges.

answers.text: Relabel one chosen vertex in a label class while leaving the others unchanged.
answers.explanation: The relabelling operation changes every vertex carrying the source label.

answers.text: Create an arbitrary nonempty labelled graph as a single atomic expression.
answers.explanation: The atomic expressions create single labelled vertices.

answers.text: Apply a same-label join $\eta_{i,i}$ as a primitive operation.
answers.explanation: The standard definition requires distinct labels. Same-label joins belong to a modified convention.

answers.text: Give one vertex several simultaneous construction labels.
answers.explanation: In the standard definition every vertex carries exactly one label at each stage.

answers.text: Join only across the two operands of a union, using their origin as an extra test.
answers.explanation: A standard clique-width join sees current labels, not which union operand a vertex came from; that origin-sensitive primitive is NLC-style.

sources.title: Ganian et al. — Shrub-depth: Capturing Height of Dense Graphs, §§2–4

questions.prompt: A class admits tree-models with a uniform height bound and a uniform finite number of leaf colours. Its graph vertices are the leaves; adjacency depends only on the two colours and their tree distance. What property is described?

answers.text: Bounded shrubdepth.
answers.explanation: Both height and colour count are uniform across the class. The tree is a model of adjacency, not a subgraph that must contain the graph.

answers.text: Bounded treewidth.
answers.explanation: Treewidth uses overlapping bags, not an adjacency interpretation on coloured leaves.

answers.text: Bounded maximum degree.
answers.explanation: A height-one model with one colour already represents arbitrarily large cliques.

answers.text: Bounded clique number.
answers.explanation: The same height-one models can represent cliques of every size.

answers.text: Bounded treedepth.
answers.explanation: Treedepth uses containment in a forest closure and excludes arbitrarily large cliques at a fixed bound.

answers.text: Bounded clique-width alone.
answers.explanation: Bounded clique-width imposes no uniform tree-model height; paths separate the two properties.

answers.text: Bounded twin-width alone.
answers.explanation: Twin-width controls red degree during contractions and does not impose this height condition.

answers.text: Bounded neighbourhood diversity alone.
answers.explanation: Neighbourhood diversity corresponds to height-one tree-models; bounded shrubdepth permits larger fixed heights.

answers.text: Bounded linear clique-width alone.
answers.explanation: Paths have bounded linear clique-width but unbounded shrubdepth.

answers.text: Bounded merge-width alone.
answers.explanation: Merge-width controls local reachability of resolved pairs, not bounded-height leaf models.

sources.title: Ganian et al. — Shrub-depth: Capturing Height of Dense Graphs, §§2–4
Dreier & Toruńczyk — Merge-width and First-Order Model Checking, Definitions 3.1–3.2 and §7 (June 2026 version)

questions.prompt: Let $\mathrm{TM}_m(d)$ denote graphs with an $m$-colour tree-model of height $d$. Which statement defines bounded shrubdepth of a class $\mathcal C$?

answers.text: $\exists d\;\exists m\;\forall G\in\mathcal C:\ G\in\mathrm{TM}_m(d)$.
answers.explanation: A single height and a single finite colour bound must work for the whole class. The actual tree and adjacency signature may vary.

answers.text: $\forall G\in\mathcal C\;\exists d,m:\ G\in\mathrm{TM}_m(d)$.
answers.explanation: Every finite graph has a height-one model using one colour per vertex. Per-graph bounds make the condition vacuous.

answers.text: $\exists d\;\forall G\in\mathcal C\;\exists m:\ G\in\mathrm{TM}_m(d)$.
answers.explanation: Choosing a different unbounded colour count for each graph again allows every graph at height one.

answers.text: $\forall d\;\exists m\;\forall G\in\mathcal C:\ G\in\mathrm{TM}_m(d)$.
answers.explanation: This demands models at every height, including height one, and is stronger than bounded shrubdepth.

answers.text: $\exists m\;\forall G\in\mathcal C\;\exists d:\ G\in\mathrm{TM}_m(d)$.
answers.explanation: The height must also be uniform. Unbounded-height one-colour models already include all cographs, whose shrubdepth is unbounded.

answers.text: $\exists d,m\;\exists G\in\mathcal C:\ G\in\mathrm{TM}_m(d)$.
answers.explanation: A model for one member gives no uniform control over the whole class.

answers.text: $\forall d,m\;\forall G\in\mathcal C:\ G\in\mathrm{TM}_m(d)$.
answers.explanation: The definition requires some sufficient bounds, not every possible choice of bounds.

answers.text: $\exists d,m\;\forall G\in\mathcal C:$ one fixed finite tree $T$ models every $G$.
answers.explanation: Tree size must be allowed to grow with the number of graph vertices.

answers.text: $\exists d,m\;\forall G\in\mathcal C:$ the model has at most $m$ leaves and height $d$.
answers.explanation: The bound is on leaf colours, not on leaf count; the class may contain arbitrarily large graphs.

answers.text: $\exists d,m\;\forall G\in\mathcal C:$ the model has height $d$ and maximum branching $m$.
answers.explanation: Bounding height and branching bounds the total number of leaves. Bounded shrubdepth does not bound graph order.

questions.prompt: In an $m$-colour tree-model of height $d$, distinct leaves $u,v$ have colours $i,j$ and distance $2\ell$. A symmetric signature $S\subseteq[m]^2\times[d]$ is given. How is adjacency defined?

answers.text: $uv\in E(G)\iff(i,j,\ell)\in S$.
answers.explanation: The signature uses the two leaf colours and half their tree distance. With all leaves at depth $d$, this is equivalent to using their least common ancestor’s depth.

answers.text: $uv\in E(G)\iff\{u,v\}\in E(T)$.
answers.explanation: Distinct leaves are not joined by a tree edge in these models. Graph adjacency is interpreted from the signature.

answers.text: $uv\in E(G)\iff i=j$, regardless of $S$.
answers.explanation: Equal-colour pairs can be adjacent or nonadjacent depending on the signature and distance.

answers.text: $uv\in E(G)\iff\ell=1$, regardless of $S$.
answers.explanation: Sibling leaves need not be adjacent, and leaves farther apart may be adjacent.

answers.text: $uv\in E(G)\iff(i,j,2\ell)\in S$.
answers.explanation: The third signature coordinate ranges over half-distances, not full tree distances.

answers.text: $uv\in E(G)\iff(i,j,d-\ell)\in S$.
answers.explanation: Here the signature was indexed by half-distance. Using least-common-ancestor depth requires translating the signature too.

answers.text: $uv\in E(G)\iff(i,j,\ell)\notin S$.
answers.explanation: This uses the complementary signature and produces the complement graph.

answers.text: $uv\in E(G)\iff\exists t\in[d]:(i,j,t)\in S$.
answers.explanation: This forgets the actual distance and may add edges intended only for other levels.

answers.text: $uv\in E(G)\iff\forall t\in[d]:(i,j,t)\in S$.
answers.explanation: Adjacency at the actual level does not require adjacency at every possible level.

answers.text: $uv\in E(G)\iff(i,i,\ell)\in S\land(j,j,\ell)\in S$.
answers.explanation: Cross-colour adjacency is its own signature entry; it need not follow from either same-colour entry.

questions.prompt: In the merge-sequence definition for a simple graph $G=(V,E)$, what conditions must $(\mathcal P_i,R_i)$ satisfy? Write $AB=\{\{a,b\}:a\in A,b\in B,a\ne b\}$.

answers.text: The partitions coarsen from singletons to $\{V\}$; $R_i\subseteq R_{i+1}$; for every $A,B\in\mathcal P_i$, including $A=B$, all pairs in $AB\setminus R_i$ are edges or all are non-edges.
answers.explanation: Resolved pairs are exceptions to a uniform default on each pair of parts. Both edges and non-edges may be resolved, and resolved pairs remain resolved.

answers.text: The partitions refine from singletons to $\{V\}$, with increasing $R_i$ and homogeneous unresolved pairs.
answers.explanation: Refinement goes towards smaller parts. Going from singletons to one part requires coarsening.

answers.text: The partitions coarsen, but every resolved pair must belong to $E$.
answers.explanation: Resolved pairs may also be non-edges; otherwise one cannot represent arbitrary exceptions to a complete default.

answers.text: The partitions coarsen and $R_i$ decreases; unresolved pairs are homogeneous.
answers.explanation: Resolution is cumulative: the sets of resolved pairs must increase, not decrease.

answers.text: The partitions coarsen and $R_i$ increases; every pair of parts must be homogeneous in the original graph, including resolved pairs.
answers.explanation: Only unresolved pairs must share a default. Resolved pairs are precisely the allowed exceptions.

answers.text: The partitions coarsen and $R_i$ increases; homogeneous unresolved pairs are required only for distinct parts.
answers.explanation: The condition also applies inside a part. Otherwise the final single part could hide arbitrary unresolved structure.

answers.text: The partitions coarsen and $R_i$ increases; every $AB\setminus R_i$ must consist only of edges.
answers.explanation: An empty-adjacency default is also allowed; the default may differ between pairs of parts.

answers.text: The partitions coarsen and $R_i$ increases; every $AB\setminus R_i$ must consist only of non-edges.
answers.explanation: Complete-adjacency defaults are allowed too; resolved pairs are not just the graph’s edges.

answers.text: The partitions coarsen and unresolved pairs are homogeneous; a pair can leave $R_i$ when its endpoints merge.
answers.explanation: Resolved pairs are original vertex pairs and remain resolved even after their parts are merged.

answers.text: The partitions coarsen and $R_i$ increases; every $AB\cap R_i$ must be homogeneous, with no restriction on $AB\setminus R_i$.
answers.explanation: The uniformity condition is on unresolved pairs, not the resolved exceptions.

questions.prompt: Let $B_r^{R_i}(v)$ be the radius-$r$ ball in $(V,R_i)$. In the merge-sequence convention allowing several merges per step, which quantity is the sequence’s radius-$r$ width?

answers.text: $\displaystyle\max_{i\ge2}\max_{v\in V}\bigl|\{A\in\mathcal P_{i-1}:A\cap B_r^{R_i}(v)\ne\varnothing\}\bigr|$.
answers.explanation: Count parts reached through resolved pairs, not vertices. Use the previous partition with the current resolved-pair set; the index offset prevents a large merge from hiding its cost.

answers.text: $\displaystyle\max_{i\ge2}\max_{v\in V}|B_r^{R_i}(v)|$.
answers.explanation: A ball may contain many vertices in one part. Width counts intersected parts instead of vertices.

answers.text: $\displaystyle\max_{i\ge2}|\mathcal P_{i-1}|$.
answers.explanation: Only parts reached from a vertex within the radius count, not every current part.

answers.text: $\displaystyle\max_{i\ge2}|R_i|$.
answers.explanation: The number of resolved pairs is not the local reachability width.

answers.text: $\displaystyle\max_{i\ge2}\max_v|\{A\in\mathcal P_i:A\cap B_r^{R_i}(v)\ne\varnothing\}|$.
answers.explanation: Using the new partition omits the required offset. A single large merge could collapse the measured count to one.

answers.text: $\displaystyle\max_{i\ge2}\max_v|\{A\in\mathcal P_{i-1}:A\cap B_r^{R_{i-1}}(v)\ne\varnothing\}|$.
answers.explanation: This measures the old resolved set and ignores pairs resolved immediately before the merge.

answers.text: $\displaystyle\max_{i\ge2}\max_v|\{A\in\mathcal P_{i-1}:A\cap B_r^G(v)\ne\varnothing\}|$.
answers.explanation: Reachability is in the resolved-pair graph, which includes resolved non-edges, not in the original graph.

answers.text: $\displaystyle\max_{i\ge2}\min_v|\{A\in\mathcal P_{i-1}:A\cap B_r^{R_i}(v)\ne\varnothing\}|$.
answers.explanation: Every vertex must satisfy the width bound; the best vertex cannot witness the maximum local complexity.

answers.text: $\displaystyle\min_{i\ge2}\max_v|\{A\in\mathcal P_{i-1}:A\cap B_r^{R_i}(v)\ne\varnothing\}|$.
answers.explanation: The sequence width is the worst stage, not the easiest stage.

answers.text: $\displaystyle\max_{i\ge2}\max_v|\{A\in\mathcal P_{i-1}:A\subseteq B_r^{R_i}(v)\}|$.
answers.explanation: Reaching one vertex of a part suffices. The ball need not contain the entire part.

questions.prompt: Fix $r$. Over valid merge sequences, minimise the maximum number of previous-partition parts reached from one original vertex by at most $r$ resolved pairs. Which graph parameter is defined?

answers.text: Radius-$r$ merge-width, $\operatorname{mw}_r(G)$.
answers.explanation: The radius is measured in the resolved-pair graph on original vertices. Optimising this local part count over merge sequences defines the parameter.

answers.text: Clique-width.
answers.explanation: Clique-width counts construction labels. It corresponds in boundedness to radius-infinity merge-width, not a fixed finite radius.

answers.text: Twin-width.
answers.explanation: Twin-width counts non-homogeneous neighbouring parts during binary contractions, rather than resolved-pair reachability.

answers.text: Shrubdepth.
answers.explanation: Shrubdepth is a uniform height condition on coloured tree-models for a graph class.

answers.text: Radius-$r$ weak colouring number.
answers.explanation: Weak colouring numbers use an order on vertices and paths in the original graph, not merge sequences and resolved pairs.

answers.text: Radius-$r$ flip-width.
answers.explanation: Flip-width uses a pursuit game with adjacency flips; this is a decomposition-based definition.

answers.text: Rank-width.
answers.explanation: Rank-width uses binary matrix ranks across cuts, not local balls of resolved pairs.

answers.text: The radius-$r$ width of one specified merge sequence.
answers.explanation: The minimum over all valid sequences is a graph parameter; a specified sequence has its own possibly larger width.

answers.text: Radius-$r$ neighbourhood complexity.
answers.explanation: Neighbourhood complexity counts distinct neighbourhood traces, not parts encountered during a construction.

answers.text: Component twin-width.
answers.explanation: Component twin-width measures red components of contraction trigraphs, not bounded-radius reachability of original vertices.

questions.prompt: What does it mean for a graph class $\mathcal C$ to have bounded merge-width, using the finite-radius parameters $\operatorname{mw}_r$?

answers.text: $\forall r\ge1\;\exists k_r\;\forall G\in\mathcal C:\ \operatorname{mw}_r(G)\le k_r$.
answers.explanation: Each fixed radius has a class-wide constant bound. That constant may depend on the radius, but not on graph order.

answers.text: $\forall G\in\mathcal C\;\forall r\ge1\;\exists k:\ \operatorname{mw}_r(G)\le k$.
answers.explanation: Every finite graph has finite width. Bounds chosen after the graph give no uniform class property.

answers.text: $\exists r\ge1\;\exists k\;\forall G\in\mathcal C:\ \operatorname{mw}_r(G)\le k$.
answers.explanation: The definition requires a bound for every fixed radius, not just one radius.

answers.text: $\exists k\;\forall r\ge1\;\forall G\in\mathcal C:\ \operatorname{mw}_r(G)\le k$.
answers.explanation: A single constant for all radii is stronger; it bounds radius-infinity merge-width and hence clique-width.

answers.text: $\forall r\ge1\;\exists c_r\;\forall G\in\mathcal C:\ \operatorname{mw}_r(G)\le c_r|V(G)|$.
answers.explanation: A linear bound in graph order is not a constant bound; indeed width is trivially at most the number of vertices.

answers.text: $\forall r\ge1\;\exists c_r\;\forall G\in\mathcal C:\ \operatorname{mw}_r(G)\le c_r\sqrt{|V(G)|}$.
answers.explanation: A bound growing with graph order does not express bounded merge-width.

answers.text: $\forall r\ge1\;\exists k_r\;\exists G\in\mathcal C:\ \operatorname{mw}_r(G)\le k_r$.
answers.explanation: The bound must hold for every graph in the class, not just a chosen graph.

answers.text: $\forall r\ge1\;\exists k_r\;\forall G\in\mathcal C:$ every merge sequence has radius-$r$ width at most $k_r$.
answers.explanation: The graph parameter minimises over sequences. Bad sequences may have large width even for a simple graph.

answers.text: $\forall r\ge1\;\exists k_r\;\forall G\in\mathcal C:$ every radius-$r$ ball in $G$ has at most $k_r$ vertices.
answers.explanation: This bounds original graph balls, excluding large cliques, although cliques have bounded merge-width.

answers.text: $\forall r\ge1\;\exists k_r\;\forall G\in\mathcal C:$ some merge sequence uses at most $k_r$ singleton parts initially.
answers.explanation: The initial singleton count is graph order. Bounded merge-width allows arbitrarily large graphs.

questions.prompt: For nonempty graphs in $\mathcal C$, which bound expresses almost bounded merge-width?

answers.text: For every fixed $r\ge1$ and $\varepsilon>0$, some $c_{r,\varepsilon}$ satisfies $\operatorname{mw}_r(G)\le c_{r,\varepsilon}|V(G)|^\varepsilon$ for all $G\in\mathcal C$.
answers.explanation: This is subpolynomial growth uniformly over the class at each fixed radius. The constant may depend on the class, radius and exponent.

answers.text: For every fixed $r$, some $c_r$ satisfies $\operatorname{mw}_r(G)\le c_r$ for all $G\in\mathcal C$.
answers.explanation: That defines bounded merge-width, which is stronger than almost bounded merge-width.

answers.text: For every fixed $r$, some $c_r$ satisfies $\operatorname{mw}_r(G)\le c_r|V(G)|$ for all $G\in\mathcal C$.
answers.explanation: Linear growth is not subpolynomial. Every graph already has width at most its order.

answers.text: For some $\varepsilon>0$ and every $r$, $\operatorname{mw}_r(G)=O(|V(G)|^\varepsilon)$ uniformly over $\mathcal C$.
answers.explanation: Almost boundedness requires every positive exponent, not one sufficiently large exponent.

answers.text: For every fixed $r$, $\operatorname{mw}_r(G)=O(\sqrt{|V(G)|})$ uniformly over $\mathcal C$.
answers.explanation: One fixed power bound does not imply bounds for all smaller positive powers.

answers.text: For every fixed $r$ and $\varepsilon>0$, each graph may choose its own constant in the bound.
answers.explanation: Allowing the constant to depend on the individual graph makes the condition vacuous.

answers.text: Only $\operatorname{mw}_1(G)$ must satisfy every positive-power bound.
answers.explanation: Almost bounded merge-width requires this at every fixed radius, not just radius one.

answers.text: For every fixed $r$, the definition requires $\operatorname{mw}_r(G)=O(\log |V(G)|)$.
answers.explanation: Logarithmic growth is a particular subpolynomial bound; it is not the defining bound in general.

answers.text: There is a single constant $c$ such that $\operatorname{mw}_r(G)\le c|V(G)|^\varepsilon$ for every $r,\varepsilon>0,G$.
answers.explanation: The constants may depend on radius and exponent. Requiring one constant imposes a much stronger condition.

answers.text: For each fixed $r$, it is enough that the average width of graphs of each order in $\mathcal C$ is subpolynomial.
answers.explanation: The bound must hold for every member, not merely on average over graphs of an order.

questions.prompt: Bounded shrubdepth implies bounded clique-width. Which class witnesses that the converse fails?

answers.text: All finite paths $\{P_n:n\ge1\}$.
answers.explanation: Paths have clique-width at most three, but no fixed tree-model height and fixed colour count can represent paths of every length.

answers.text: All cliques $\{K_n:n\ge1\}$.
answers.explanation: Cliques have height-one, one-colour tree-models, so their shrubdepth is bounded.

answers.text: All edgeless graphs.
answers.explanation: Use height one, one colour, and an empty adjacency signature.

answers.text: All complete bipartite graphs $K_{a,b}$.
answers.explanation: Two colours on a height-one tree distinguish the sides; the signature joins exactly different colours.

answers.text: All stars.
answers.explanation: Stars are complete bipartite graphs with one side of size one, so height one and two colours suffice.

answers.text: All disjoint unions of edges and isolated vertices.
answers.explanation: A height-two model groups the two endpoints of each edge; one colour and adjacency only within a group suffice.

answers.text: All disjoint unions of cliques.
answers.explanation: A height-two model groups vertices by clique; use one colour and join exactly leaves in the same group.

answers.text: All complements of matchings.
answers.explanation: A height-two model groups matched pairs; its signature joins leaves from different groups.

answers.text: All disjoint unions of stars.
answers.explanation: Use height-two groups for components and two colours for centres and leaves; join unlike colours only inside a group.

answers.text: All complete multipartite graphs.
answers.explanation: A height-two, one-colour model groups each independent part and joins leaves exactly across different groups.

questions.prompt: For classes of finite simple graphs, what is the relation between bounded clique-width and bounded twin-width?

answers.text: Bounded clique-width implies bounded twin-width; the converse fails, for example on square grids.
answers.explanation: Clique-width bounds yield twin-width bounds. Square grids have uniformly bounded twin-width but unbounded clique-width.

answers.text: Bounded twin-width implies bounded clique-width, but not conversely.
answers.explanation: The implication is in the other direction; square grids refute the proposed implication.

answers.text: The two boundedness properties are equivalent.
answers.explanation: Square grids have bounded twin-width and unbounded clique-width.

answers.text: Neither boundedness property implies the other.
answers.explanation: Every class of bounded clique-width has bounded twin-width.

answers.text: Bounded clique-width implies bounded twin-width only for sparse classes.
answers.explanation: The implication holds also for dense graphs; no sparsity hypothesis is needed.

answers.text: Bounded clique-width implies bounded twin-width only for hereditary classes.
answers.explanation: The parameter bound applies to individual graphs and hence to any class, without a closure hypothesis.

answers.text: Bounded twin-width implies bounded clique-width for all bipartite classes.
answers.explanation: Square grids are bipartite and still have unbounded clique-width.

answers.text: Bounded twin-width implies bounded clique-width for all planar classes.
answers.explanation: The square-grid counterexample is already planar.

answers.text: Bounded twin-width implies bounded clique-width for all classes of maximum degree at most four.
answers.explanation: Square grids have maximum degree at most four.

answers.text: The parameters are numerically equal on every graph.
answers.explanation: Even a clique with at least two vertices has twin-width zero and clique-width two.

questions.prompt: For unordered finite simple graph classes, what is the relation between bounded twin-width and bounded merge-width?

answers.text: Bounded twin-width implies bounded merge-width; the converse fails even for the class of graphs of maximum degree at most three.
answers.explanation: A bounded-red-degree contraction sequence gives bounds at each finite radius. Bounded-degree classes have bounded merge-width, while subcubic graphs have unbounded twin-width.

answers.text: Bounded merge-width implies bounded twin-width, but not conversely.
answers.explanation: The direction is reversed; the class of subcubic graphs refutes this implication.

answers.text: The two properties are equivalent for all unordered graph classes.
answers.explanation: Subcubic graphs give a counterexample to equivalence.

answers.text: The properties are incomparable.
answers.explanation: Bounded twin-width always implies bounded merge-width.

answers.text: The implication from twin-width to merge-width requires bounded clique-width as well.
answers.explanation: A bounded twin-width sequence suffices; no clique-width bound is needed.

answers.text: Bounded merge-width implies bounded twin-width whenever the class is hereditary.
answers.explanation: The class of all graphs of maximum degree at most three is hereditary and refutes this.

answers.text: Bounded merge-width implies bounded twin-width whenever the class has bounded maximum degree.
answers.explanation: Subcubic graphs have a fixed maximum-degree bound but unbounded twin-width.

answers.text: Bounded twin-width supplies one constant that bounds merge-width simultaneously at every radius, including infinity.
answers.explanation: A uniform infinity-radius bound would imply bounded clique-width, which square grids refute.

answers.text: Bounded twin-width supplies finite-radius merge-width bounds only after choosing an order as an extra input relation.
answers.explanation: The implication already holds for unordered graphs. An order is not required.

answers.text: The ordered-graph equivalence proves equivalence after simply forgetting the order on any bounded-merge-width graph.
answers.explanation: One must control the width of the ordered expansion. An unordered bound alone does not supply such an expansion.

questions.prompt: Extend resolved-pair reachability to $r=\infty$, so an entire connected component can be reached. Which class property is equivalent to $\sup_{G\in\mathcal C}\operatorname{mw}_\infty(G)<\infty$?

answers.text: Bounded clique-width.
answers.explanation: The infinity-radius parameter is functionally equivalent to clique-width. Bounds at each fixed finite radius are weaker than one bound on whole resolved components.

answers.text: Bounded maximum degree.
answers.explanation: Cliques have bounded clique-width and infinity-radius merge-width but unbounded maximum degree.

answers.text: Bounded clique number.
answers.explanation: Cliques again have bounded infinity-radius merge-width but unbounded clique number.

answers.text: Bounded treewidth.
answers.explanation: Cliques have bounded clique-width but unbounded treewidth.

answers.text: Bounded twin-width.
answers.explanation: Square grids have bounded twin-width but unbounded clique-width, and therefore unbounded infinity-radius merge-width.

answers.text: Bounded merge-width at each fixed finite radius.
answers.explanation: Square grids have bounded merge-width at every fixed finite radius but unbounded clique-width.

answers.text: Monadic dependence.
answers.explanation: Monadic dependence includes square grids and many classes of unbounded clique-width.

answers.text: Bounded shrubdepth.
answers.explanation: Paths have bounded clique-width, hence bounded infinity-radius merge-width, but unbounded shrubdepth.

answers.text: Bounded linear clique-width.
answers.explanation: This is stronger than bounded clique-width; for example cographs have bounded clique-width but unbounded linear clique-width.

answers.text: Bounded neighbourhood diversity.
answers.explanation: Paths have bounded clique-width and unbounded neighbourhood diversity.

questions.prompt: For a hereditary class $\mathcal C$ (closed under induced subgraphs), what relationship follows from the merge-width results, including the 4 November 2026 preprint?

answers.text: $\mathcal C$ is monadically dependent if and only if it has almost bounded merge-width.
answers.explanation: The November preprint proves dependence implies almost bounded merge-width. The reverse implication for hereditary classes was already known. “Almost bounded” means subpolynomial at every fixed radius.

answers.text: $\mathcal C$ is monadically dependent if and only if it has bounded clique-width.
answers.explanation: Square grids and their induced subgraphs are monadically dependent but have unbounded clique-width.

answers.text: $\mathcal C$ is monadically dependent if and only if it has bounded twin-width.
answers.explanation: The hereditary class of all subcubic graphs is dependent but has unbounded twin-width.

answers.text: $\mathcal C$ is monadically dependent if and only if it has bounded shrubdepth.
answers.explanation: All linear forests form a hereditary dependent class containing arbitrarily long paths, so shrubdepth is unbounded.

answers.text: $\mathcal C$ is monadically dependent if and only if it has bounded merge-width.
answers.explanation: Dependence permits unbounded merge-width: nowhere dense classes with unbounded expansion are examples.

answers.text: The implication from dependence to almost bounded merge-width remains conjectural at every radius.
answers.explanation: The cited November 2026 preprint states and proves it for every fixed radius.

answers.text: The November result proves the implication only at radius one.
answers.explanation: The earlier July 2026 result handled radius one; the November theorem handles every fixed radius.

answers.text: The result replaces “every positive exponent” with “one fixed positive exponent” in the width bound.
answers.explanation: Almost boundedness means every positive exponent, with constants allowed to depend on that exponent.

answers.text: The result gives one subpolynomial bound uniform over all radii simultaneously.
answers.explanation: The subpolynomial function may depend on the fixed radius. Uniform control of arbitrarily large radii is not asserted.

answers.text: The result says that every merge sequence of every graph in the class has subpolynomial width.
answers.explanation: It asserts existence of suitable sequences and gives an algorithm to find them. Bad sequences may still have large width.

questions.prompt: Which condition characterises bounded shrubdepth using first-order transductions?

answers.text: The class is contained in the outputs of one fixed FO transduction of finite rooted trees whose height has a uniform bound.
answers.explanation: A bounded-height tree-model gives such a transduction using finitely many colours. Conversely, fixed FO interpretations of bounded-height coloured trees have bounded shrubdepth.

answers.text: The class is contained in the outputs of fixed FO transductions of arbitrary finite graphs.
answers.explanation: This is vacuous: the identity transduction already covers every graph class.

answers.text: Every member is a subgraph of some rooted tree of bounded height.
answers.explanation: This excludes dense examples such as cliques. A transduction can create adjacency between leaves.

answers.text: Every member is a minor of some rooted tree of bounded height.
answers.explanation: Minors of trees are forests, so this cannot cover bounded-shrubdepth classes containing triangles.

answers.text: The class is transducible from finite rooted trees of arbitrary height, with no other restriction.
answers.explanation: The identity on all paths already gives an unbounded-shrubdepth output class. A uniform height bound is essential.

answers.text: The class transduces some bounded-height trees.
answers.explanation: This reverses the direction and is too weak: even very complicated classes can output an edgeless graph or one vertex.

answers.text: Each output graph has its own FO transduction from a height-one tree, with no uniform formula bound.
answers.explanation: Any fixed finite graph can be encoded with sufficiently many specially chosen colours. The recipe must be uniform across the class.

answers.text: The class is transducible from trees of bounded degree, allowing unbounded height.
answers.explanation: Paths have bounded degree but unbounded shrubdepth, and the identity transduction preserves them.

answers.text: A fixed FO transduction from bounded-height trees must preserve the original tree edges on its output vertices.
answers.explanation: The interpretation may completely redefine adjacency. Requiring inherited tree edges would rule out dense examples.

answers.text: One fixed finite rooted tree must supply all outputs, although their vertex counts can be unbounded.
answers.explanation: Fixed finite copying and interpretation cannot produce arbitrarily large outputs from one fixed finite input.

questions.prompt: Let $H_n$ be the half-graph with sides $a_1,\ldots,a_n$ and $b_1,\ldots,b_n$, with $a_i b_j$ an edge iff $i\le j$. Which distinction between monadic dependence and monadic stability is correct?

answers.text: Dependence forbids transducing all finite graphs; stability forbids transducing all half-graphs and is the stronger condition.
answers.explanation: A recipe for all graphs would also produce all half-graphs. Half-graphs themselves have bounded clique-width and are dependent, but are not monadically stable.

answers.text: Dependence forbids all half-graphs; stability forbids all finite graphs and is weaker.
answers.explanation: The two forbidden target families are exchanged.

answers.text: Dependence and stability both forbid only arbitrarily large cliques.
answers.explanation: Cliques can have both properties; the obstructions concern logical encodings of graphs or half-graphs.

answers.text: Dependence and stability are the same property on every graph class.
answers.explanation: The class of all half-graphs is dependent but fails stability via the identity transduction.

answers.text: Stability merely forbids half-graphs as non-induced subgraphs.
answers.explanation: The condition concerns FO transductions, not ordinary subgraph containment.

answers.text: Stability merely forbids half-graphs as induced subgraphs.
answers.explanation: Absence as induced subgraphs alone does not exclude half-graphs obtainable through a logical encoding.

answers.text: Monadic dependence implies monadic stability, with half-graphs as a witness.
answers.explanation: Half-graphs show the opposite: they are dependent but not stable.

answers.text: The half-graph class is monadically independent because its adjacency encodes an order.
answers.explanation: An order pattern witnesses instability, not the independence needed to encode all finite graphs.

answers.text: Stability forbids each half-graph separately, even when a different transduction is chosen for each size.
answers.explanation: The obstruction is one uniform transduction producing half-graphs of every size, not separate recipes for each size.

answers.text: Only transductions without added unary predicates count in either definition.
answers.explanation: Both monadic notions allow arbitrary finite unary expansions.

questions.prompt: What happens to twin-width under complementation of a finite simple graph $G$?

answers.text: $\operatorname{tww}(\overline G)=\operatorname{tww}(G)$: the same partition sequence has the same red graphs.
answers.explanation: Complementation swaps complete and empty pairs of parts, while mixed pairs remain mixed. Thus every sequence keeps exactly the same red degrees.

answers.text: $\operatorname{tww}(\overline G)=\operatorname{tww}(G)+1$ for every nonempty $G$.
answers.explanation: Complementing twice would increase the value by two while returning to the original graph.

answers.text: $\operatorname{tww}(\overline G)=|V(G)|-1-\operatorname{tww}(G)$.
answers.explanation: A clique and an edgeless graph both have twin-width zero, refuting this formula.

answers.text: $\operatorname{tww}(\overline G)=0$ for every $G$.
answers.explanation: Complementation is an involution, so this would incorrectly give twin-width zero to every graph.

answers.text: A red pair becomes black because a mixed adjacency relation becomes complete.
answers.explanation: Complementing a mixture of edges and non-edges leaves another mixture, not a complete relation.

answers.text: Every black pair becomes red because all its adjacencies change.
answers.explanation: Changing a complete pair to an empty pair preserves homogeneity; it creates no red edge.

answers.text: Every non-edge pair becomes red because new edges are introduced.
answers.explanation: An empty pair becomes complete and remains homogeneous.

answers.text: Equality is guaranteed only for graphs of bounded maximum degree.
answers.explanation: The homogeneity argument applies to every finite simple graph, irrespective of degree.

answers.text: Equality requires a different contraction sequence and fails for the original optimal sequence.
answers.explanation: The same sequence preserves exactly which pairs of parts are mixed.

answers.text: Complementation preserves only the total red-edge count; individual red degrees can change along the same partition sequence.
answers.explanation: The whole red graph is unchanged at each partition, so every individual red degree is unchanged too.
